eyebrow: KEY STAGE 3 HISTORY • YEAR 8 ENQUIRY CHRONOLOGY • 15 MILESTONES

eras.title: Part 1: Chartered Companies, Plantation Slavery & Maroon Resistance (1600–1740)
Part 2: Conquest of Bengal & Crisis in the Thirteen Colonies (1756–1773)
Part 3: American Independence, Black Loyalists & Slave Trade Abolition (1775–1807)

milestones.title: Queen Elizabeth I Grants the East India Company Charter
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did a London trading company seize military control of Mughal Bengal?
milestones.imageCaption: East India House on Leadenhall Street, London: Headquarters of the joint-stock monopoly chartered by Queen Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: East India Company coastal factories across Mughal India and the conquest of Bengal (1600–1765).
milestones.catalyst: Eager to break into lucrative Asian spice and textile markets, **218 London merchants** pooled **£68,000** to fit out armed ocean-going galleons carrying silver bullion.
milestones.turningPoint: On **New Year’s Eve 1600**, Queen Elizabeth I granted an exclusive royal **monopoly charter** creating **The East India Company (EIC)** under commander James Lancaster.
milestones.impact: Early voyages returning with pepper and cotton earned profits above **300%**, fusing private City finance with royal state backing.
milestones.bridgeToNext: To trade permanently on the Indian mainland, English merchants had to seek permission from the mighty Mughal Emperor.

keyTerms.definition: A formal royal document granting exclusive trading rights, legal powers, or land to a private corporation.
Complete and exclusive control over the trade or supply of a specific commodity in a given region.

milestones.title: Sir Thomas Roe & Fortified Mughal Coastal Factories
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did a London trading company seize military control of Mughal Bengal?
milestones.imageCaption: Sir Thomas Roe (National Portrait Gallery): Ambassador sent by King James I to Emperor Jahangir’s Mughal court in 1615 to secure Surat factory rights.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Fortified East India Company trading factories established at Surat, Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta.
milestones.catalyst: Mughal India produced a quarter of the world’s manufactured goods, making English merchants petitioners at a far wealthier Asian empire’s court.
milestones.turningPoint: Dispatched by James I in **1615**, ambassador **Sir Thomas Roe** persuaded Mughal **Emperor Jahangir** to permit permanent English warehouses (**factories**) at **Surat**.
milestones.impact: Over the seventeenth century, the Company expanded fortified coastal bases across **Surat, Madras, Bombay, and Calcutta**, guarded by privately hired **sepoy** infantry.
milestones.bridgeToNext: While trading textiles in Asia, England expanded westward in 1655 by seizing Caribbean sugar territory from Spain.

keyTerms.definition: In early modern trade, a fortified commercial trading post and warehouse managed by a company "factor".
An Indian soldier recruited, armed, and trained under European officers to fight in the East India Company’s army.

milestones.title: Cromwell’s Seizure of Jamaica & Birth of the Free Maroons
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did enslaved Africans and Queen Nanny resist plantation slavery in Jamaica?
milestones.imageCaption: Edward Barlow’s seventeenth-century chart of Port Royal harbour and Jamaica’s rugged Blue Mountains (Royal Museums Greenwich).
milestones.catalyst: Seeking wealthy Caribbean colonies under his **Western Design**, Oliver Cromwell sent an English expeditionary fleet against Spanish-ruled **Jamaica** in **1655**.
milestones.turningPoint: Amid the chaos of England’s invasion, enslaved Africans broke free and escaped into Jamaica’s forested **Blue Mountains** to establish autonomous **Maroon** towns.
milestones.impact: While British planters turned coastal plains into brutal **sugar monoculture** estates, free Maroon strongholds defied colonial recapture from the mountain interior.
milestones.bridgeToNext: To feed labour-hungry Caribbean sugar estates, the Stuart Crown organized a royal slave-trading monopoly in West Africa.

keyTerms.definition: A self-liberated formerly enslaved African who established independent, fortified free settlements in remote wilderness.
A large commercial agricultural estate dedicated to the monoculture cultivation of cash crops like sugar or tobacco.

milestones.title: The Royal African Company, Triangular Trade & The 1713 Asiento
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the transatlantic slave trade operate, and how was it challenged?
milestones.imageCaption: Coastal slave fortress at Elmina on the Gold Coast (Ghana), where kidnapped captives were imprisoned in barracoons before Atlantic embarkation.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The Transatlantic Triangular Trade linking Bristol and Liverpool, West African forts, and American plantations.
milestones.catalyst: Ships from **London, Bristol, and Liverpool** carried guns, iron bars, and textiles to West Africa in a lucrative **triangular trade** for human captives.
milestones.turningPoint: King Charles II chartered **The Royal African Company (RAC)** in **1672**—branding captives **‘RAC’** on the chest—before Britain won Spain’s **1713 Asiento** slave-supply contract.
milestones.impact: Royal backing made Britain the dominant **transatlantic slave-trading power**, enriching British ports, banks, and Caribbean planters.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Millions of kidnapped African men, women, and children were forced below deck onto the deadly Middle Passage and sugar gangs.

keyTerms.definition: The three-legged commercial trade system connecting Britain, West Africa, and the American plantation colonies.
The lucrative monopoly contract granted by the Spanish Crown to supply 4,800 enslaved people per year to Spanish America.
A fortified coastal cage or holding pen where captured Africans were imprisoned before being loaded onto ships.

milestones.title: The Middle Passage, Sugar Gang System & Everyday Resistance
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the transatlantic slave trade operate, and how was it challenged?
milestones.imageCaption: Cutaway painting of the cramped slave deck aboard La Marie-Séraphique (1770, Musée d’Histoire de Nantes), showing captives chained below deck.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Middle Passage ocean crossings to Caribbean sugar islands and North American colonies.
milestones.catalyst: Treated legally as **chattel property**, captive Africans endured an eight-week **Middle Passage** chained on airless wooden shelves where roughly **one in six died** of dysentery and fever.
milestones.turningPoint: Survivors sold onto Jamaican sugar plantations worked **18-hour harvest shifts** under whip-wielding **overseers** beside crushing rollers and scalding boiling houses.
milestones.impact: Enslaved communities resisted daily by breaking tools, slowing production, preserving West African herbal medicine, and telling **Anansi** trickster stories.
milestones.bridgeToNext: High in Jamaica’s Blue Mountains, Queen Nanny turned resistance into full-scale guerrilla war against British regiments.

keyTerms.definition: The traumatic sea crossing of the Atlantic Ocean transporting captive enslaved Africans to the Americas.
A legal system where human beings are owned, bought, and sold as permanent private property like livestock.
The division of enslaved field labourers into work gangs based on physical strength, driven by armed drivers with whips.

milestones.title: Queen Nanny’s Guerrilla War & The 1739 Maroon Peace Treaty
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did enslaved Africans and Queen Nanny resist plantation slavery in Jamaica?
milestones.imageCaption: Old Cudjoe Making Peace (1739 engraving): Maroon commander Captain Cudjoe negotiates the 1739 Articles of Pacification with British officers.
milestones.catalyst: British colonial troops marched repeatedly into Jamaica’s rugged interior to destroy free **Windward and Leeward Maroon** towns during the First Maroon War.
milestones.turningPoint: Asante leader **Queen Nanny** defeated British soldiers using **living-branch camouflage** and **abeng** cow-horn signals, forcing Governor Trelawny to sign the **1739 Peace Treaty**.
milestones.impact: Britain recognized Maroon **freedom** and **1,500 sovereign acres**, though the treaty forced a painful compromise requiring Maroons to return future plantation runaways.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Seventeen years later, imperial war shifted eastward as the East India Company clashed with the Nawab of Bengal.

keyTerms.definition: Irregular military tactics involving fast ambushes, camouflage, hit-and-run raids, and exploiting rugged terrain.
A hollowed cow-horn instrument used by Jamaican Maroons to communicate coded tactical signals across mountain valleys.

milestones.title: Calcutta Crisis, Mir Jafar’s Betrayal & The Battle of Plassey
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did a London trading company seize military control of Mughal Bengal?
milestones.imageCaption: Tactical survey plan of the Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757), showing Robert Clive’s troops facing Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah’s army along the Bhagirathi River.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Fort William (Calcutta) and Robert Clive’s campaign culminating at the Battle of Plassey (June 1757).
milestones.catalyst: When Company officials mounted unauthorized cannons on Calcutta’s **Fort William** in **1756**, young **Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah** stormed the fort, followed by deaths in the **Black Hole** dungeon.
milestones.turningPoint: **Robert Clive** secretly bribed Bengal army commander **Mir Jafar** with promises of the throne and kept British gunpowder dry under tarpaulins to win the **Battle of Plassey** on **23 June 1757**.
milestones.impact: Installing Mir Jafar as a **puppet ruler** turned a London merchant company into the military kingmaker of rich Mughal Bengal.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Winning global battles against France in India and North America left Britain triumphant in 1763—but buried under £133 million of war debt.

keyTerms.definition: A semi-independent provincial governor or Muslim ruler within the Mughal Empire, such as the ruler of Bengal.
A figurehead ruler who appears sovereign but is secretly directed and manipulated by an outside imperial power.

milestones.title: Seven Years’ War Debt & The 1763 Proclamation Line
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did British taxes push the Thirteen Colonies toward open rebellion by 1773?
milestones.imageCaption: Official broadside of King George III’s Royal Proclamation of 7 October 1763 banning colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: The Thirteen Colonies and King George III’s 1763 Royal Proclamation Line along the Appalachian Mountains.
milestones.catalyst: Victory in the **Seven Years’ War** handed Britain vast North American territory from France, but burdened London with a crushing **£133 million war debt**.
milestones.turningPoint: To prevent costly frontier wars with Native American nations, **King George III** issued the **Proclamation of 1763** barring white settlement west of the **Appalachians** alongside **Quartering Acts**.
milestones.impact: American colonists felt cheated out of western lands they had fought for and resented housing **10,000 British redcoats** in peacetime.
milestones.bridgeToNext: To make colonists help pay for imperial defence, Parliament introduced a direct tax on paper across America in March 1765.

keyTerms.definition: The forced housing and feeding of military troops in civilian barns, taverns, or unoccupied buildings.
A colloquial 18th-century term for a British soldier, named after their distinctive scarlet wool uniform jackets.

milestones.title: The 1765 Stamp Act & ‘No Taxation Without Representation’
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did British taxes push the Thirteen Colonies toward open rebellion by 1773?
milestones.imageCaption: Skull-and-crossbones Stamp Act protest emblem from William Bradford’s Pennsylvania Journal (31 October 1765).
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Port cities across the Thirteen Colonies where Sons of Liberty boycotts defeated the 1765 Stamp Act.
milestones.catalyst: In **March 1765**, Parliament passed the **Stamp Act**, requiring revenue stamps on colonial newspapers, legal documents, pamphlets, and playing cards.
milestones.turningPoint: Declaring **‘no taxation without representation’**, the **Sons of Liberty** intimidated stamp agents and organized sweeping **boycotts** of British imports.
milestones.impact: Slumping trade forced Parliament to **repeal** the Stamp Act in **1766**, while uniting the Thirteen Colonies around a shared protest network.
milestones.bridgeToNext: That same summer of 1765, halfway across the world, the East India Company seized formal tax rule over twenty million people in Bengal.

keyTerms.definition: A concerted commercial protest refusing to purchase goods from a particular country or merchant.
A radical grassroots organisation formed in American port cities to resist British imperial taxation.
The official parliamentary revocation, cancellation, or withdrawal of a statute law.

milestones.title: The 1765 Diwani Treaty of Allahabad & The 1770 Bengal Famine
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did a London trading company seize military control of Mughal Bengal?
milestones.imageCaption: Benjamin West, Shah ‘Alam Conveying the Grant of the Diwani to Lord Clive, August 1765: Handing Bengal’s land-tax revenues to the East India Company.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Buxar and the August 1765 Diwani grant across Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
milestones.catalyst: Following further Company battlefield victories at Buxar, Robert Clive cornered Mughal **Emperor Shah Alam II** into signing the **Treaty of Allahabad** in **August 1765**.
milestones.turningPoint: The treaty granted the Company the **Diwani**—the sovereign legal right to collect land taxes across **Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa**.
milestones.impact: Relentless Company tax extraction during severe drought worsened the **1770 Bengal Famine**, in which roughly **ten million people** died while Company debts mounted in London.
milestones.bridgeToNext: To bail out the debt-ridden East India Company’s 18 million pounds of unsold tea, Parliament passed the 1773 Tea Act—igniting Boston.

keyTerms.definition: The sovereign constitutional right to collect land revenues and administer civil justice across Bengal.
The violent or corrupt extraction of wealth, goods, and tax revenues from a conquered people.

milestones.title: The Boston Massacre, 1773 Tea Act & The Boston Tea Party
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did British taxes push the Thirteen Colonies toward open rebellion by 1773?
milestones.imageCaption: W. D. Cooper, Americans Throwing the Cargoes of the Tea Ships into the River, at Boston (1789, Library of Congress): Dumping 342 chests of tea on 16 December 1773.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Boston Harbour, Griffin’s Wharf, and the 1774 Coercive Acts clampdown on Massachusetts.
milestones.catalyst: Anger after the **March 1770 Boston Massacre**—where five died including **Crispus Attucks**—boiled over when the **May 1773 Tea Act** gave the East India Company a colonial tea monopoly.
milestones.turningPoint: On **16 December 1773**, **Sons of Liberty** disguised as Mohawks boarded three ships in Boston Harbour and dumped **342 chests** (£10,000) of tea into the sea.
milestones.impact: King George III retaliated with the **1774 Coercive Acts**, closing Boston port, suspending Massachusetts self-government, and pushing the colonies to armed revolt.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Sixteen months later, musket fire on Lexington Green turned tax protests into an all-out Revolutionary War.

keyTerms.definition: A series of punitive laws passed by British Parliament in 1774 to punish Massachusetts for the Boston Tea Party.
Information, imagery, or rumours deliberately spread to influence public opinion and provoke political outrage.

milestones.title: Lexington, Dunmore’s Offer & The 1776 Declaration of Independence
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the American Revolution win independence while leaving slavery intact?
milestones.imageCaption: John Trumbull, Declaration of Independence (US Capitol): Thomas Jefferson and the Committee of Five present the draft Declaration in July 1776.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Lexington and Concord (April 1775), Virginia’s Dunmore Proclamation, and Philadelphia’s 1776 Continental Congress.
milestones.catalyst: Fighting erupted at **Lexington and Concord in April 1775**, while Virginia Governor **Lord Dunmore** promised freedom to enslaved people who fled rebel masters to join British lines.
milestones.turningPoint: Inspired by Thomas Paine’s *Common Sense*, **Thomas Jefferson** drafted the **4 July 1776 Declaration of Independence** proclaiming that **‘all men are created equal’**.
milestones.impact: Yet **41 of the 56 signatories** owned enslaved people, exposing a stark paradox that left half a million African Americans in bondage inside the new republic.
milestones.bridgeToNext: To defeat Britain’s powerful army and navy, George Washington’s Patriots needed European superpower allies.
keyAgents: Lord Dunmore’s Ethiopian Regiment & The Black Loyalists

keyTerms.definition: Fundamental human rights (such as life, liberty, and happiness) that cannot be taken away or surrendered to any government.
Claiming to have moral principles or beliefs to which one’s own actual behaviour and actions do not conform.

milestones.title: Saratoga, French Intervention & British Surrender at Yorktown
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the American Revolution win independence while leaving slavery intact?
milestones.imageCaption: John Trumbull, Surrender of Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia (19 October 1781): 8,000 besieged British troops lay down their arms.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: American victory at Saratoga (1777) and the Franco-American trap at Yorktown on Chesapeake Bay (October 1781).
milestones.catalyst: General Burgoyne’s surrender at **Saratoga in October 1777** persuaded **King Louis XVI’s France** to enter the war, forcing Britain to divert warships to guard rich Caribbean sugar islands.
milestones.turningPoint: In **October 1781**, **George Washington’s** army by land and **Admiral de Grasse’s** French fleet in Chesapeake Bay trapped **Lord Cornwallis** into surrendering **8,000 redcoats** at **Yorktown**.
milestones.impact: Yorktown shattered Parliament’s political will to fight on in North America and forced London to open peace talks.
milestones.bridgeToNext: As British diplomats signed peace in Paris in 1783, 3,000 Black Loyalists in New York demanded the freedom Britain had promised them.

keyTerms.definition: The entry of foreign military powers (such as France and Spain) into a conflict to aid one of the warring sides.
A military force raised from the civilian population to supplement a regular army in times of emergency.

milestones.title: The 1783 Treaty of Paris & The Book of Negroes Evacuation
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the American Revolution win independence while leaving slavery intact?
milestones.imageCaption: Inspection pass from The Book of Negroes (1783), certifying an emancipated Black Loyalist to board British evacuation ships in New York Harbour.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: 1783 evacuation of 3,000 Black Loyalists from New York Harbour to Birchtown and Shelburne in Nova Scotia.
milestones.catalyst: Signed on **3 September 1783**, the **Treaty of Paris** formally recognized the United States of America and ended the First British Empire in the Thirteen Colonies.
milestones.turningPoint: Refusing George Washington’s demand to return formerly enslaved soldiers, British commander **Sir Guy Carleton** registered **3,000 Black Loyalists** in the **Book of Negroes** and evacuated them to **Nova Scotia**.
milestones.impact: Black Loyalists forged free communities in Canada and later **Freetown, Sierra Leone**, while Britain pivoted its imperial ambitions eastward toward India.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Shocked by the 1781 Zong atrocity and American hypocrisy, British and African campaigners now mobilized to outlaw the slave trade itself.
keyAgents: Lord Dunmore’s Ethiopian Regiment & The Black Loyalists

keyTerms.definition: The 1783 peace agreement in which Great Britain formally recognised the independence of the United States of America.
An enslaved African who escaped rebel masters to fight for the British Crown in exchange for guaranteed freedom.

milestones.title: The Zong Outrage, Olaudah Equiano & The 1807 Abolition Act
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the transatlantic slave trade operate, and how was it challenged?
milestones.imageCaption: Frontispiece portrait from The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano (1789), whose testimony galvanized British abolitionism.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Transatlantic slave-trading routes outlawed for British vessels under Parliament’s 1807 Abolition Act.
milestones.catalyst: Public outrage erupted after Captain Luke Collingwood threw **133 sick captives** off the slave ship **Zong in November 1781** so the owners could claim cargo insurance.
milestones.turningPoint: Freed African author **Olaudah Equiano** published his **1789 autobiography** alongside **Thomas Clarkson’s** tours, Wedgwood’s medallion, and the **1788 *Brookes* ship diagram**.
milestones.impact: Mass petitions and testimony forced Parliament to pass the **Abolition of the Slave Trade Act in 1807**, outlawing human trafficking on British ships.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Lasting Legacy: Losing the Thirteen Colonies ended the First British Empire in 1783, yet Company rule in India and Caribbean slavery persisted past 1807.

keyTerms.definition: A campaigner or activist who campaigned to legally ban the slave trade and emancipate enslaved people.
Using detailed, factual, and scientific evidence to investigate crimes, abuses, or historical atrocities.
